title: Reverse String
summary: You get a string stored as a list of single characters, `s`. Reverse it in place: rearrange the characters inside `s` itself so its first character ends up last, its second ends up second to last, and so on. Return nothing, and use only O(1) extra space, so don't build a second list.

examples.explanation: Nothing is returned: s itself now holds the characters in reverse order.
With an odd length, the middle "r" stays where it is.

constraints: every s[i] is a printable ASCII character

approaches.twist: Swap the characters at both ends, then move both pointers inward until they meet.
Build a reversed copy with s[::-1] and write it back into s.
approaches.note: Works in O(n) time, but the reversed copy takes O(n) extra space. The target is O(1).

approaches.twist: Push every character onto a stack, then pop them back into s from the front.
approaches.note: Works in O(n) time, but the stack holds a copy of every character: O(n) extra space. The target is O(1).

signals.meaning: You change s itself instead of returning a new list, so characters can only trade places inside s: the two ends first, then the next pair in.
Each character trades places with its mirror at the other end. Those mirrored pairs are exactly what two pointers from both ends visit.
A reversed copy, s[::-1] or a stack all hold n characters. Two indexes and one swap at a time need no extra room.

constraintReading: len(s) can reach 10⁵, and every character except a middle one has to move, so O(n) is both needed and enough. The O(1) extra space rule is the real limit: it rules out a reversed copy or a stack, so swap in place with two indexes.

related.relation: Same pointers from both ends meeting in the middle, but it compares each mirrored pair instead of swapping it.
